title: THE TERRIFYING REASON JESUS SAID THE FIRST WILL BE LAST—AND WHY SOME PEOPLE WHO THINK THEY'RE CLOSEST TO HEAVEN MAY BE THE MOST SURPRISED
paragraphs: THE TERRIFYING REASON JESUS SAID THE FIRST WILL BE LAST—AND WHY SOME PEOPLE WHO THINK THEY'RE CLOSEST TO HEAVEN MAY BE THE MOST SURPRISED

What if the person everyone overlooks is closer to the heart of God than the person everyone applauds? Jesus spoke a warning that shattered religious pride, exposed hidden motives, and revealed a grace that human beings still struggle to understand.
There is something deeply unsettling about standing before God after spending your entire life believing you were ahead of everyone else… only to discover that you misunderstood what mattered most.
Imagine it.
A man walks into eternity carrying the memory of every religious accomplishment he ever achieved.
Every sermon he preached.
Every offering he gave.
Every ministry he led.
Every person who called him a great servant of God.
He expects applause.
But then he notices someone standing nearby.
A woman nobody remembered.

She never stood behind a pulpit. Never became famous. Never had thousands following her. She spent years caring for her sick mother, praying through exhaustion, forgiving people who never apologized, and quietly trusting Jesus when life gave her every reason to walk away.
Nobody knew her name.
But God knew every tear.
And suddenly, the man begins to understand something he had read in Scripture a hundred times but had never truly allowed to confront his heart.
“But many that are first shall be last; and the last shall be first.” — Matthew 19:30 (KJV)
That imagined scene is not a description of an actual heavenly judgment recorded in Scripture. It is a picture meant to bring us face-to-face with a very real warning from Jesus.
Because what if the greatest danger in your Christian life is not that you have done too little for God…
…but that you have slowly begun believing God owes you something for everything you have done?
Read that again.
And don't rush past it.
Because the words of Jesus were not merely about changing positions in heaven.
They were about exposing the human heart.
And the story behind those words makes them even more disturbing.
A wealthy young man once approached Jesus with a question that sounded deeply spiritual.
“Good Master, what good thing shall I do, that I may have eternal life?” (Matthew 19:16, KJV)
He was serious enough to approach Jesus. He was morally disciplined. He had kept commandments from his youth, according to his own testimony.
From the outside, he looked like someone who had everything going for him.
Successful.
Respectable.
Religious.
The kind of person a congregation might admire.
But Jesus saw something beneath his impressive exterior.
Something that had quietly occupied the throne of his heart.
His wealth.
Jesus told him to sell his possessions, give to the poor, and follow Him, promising treasure in heaven (Matthew 19:21).
And Scripture records one of the saddest departures in the Gospels.
“But when the young man heard that saying, he went away sorrowful: for he had great possessions.” (Matthew 19:22, KJV)
He came looking for eternal life.
He stood before the One who is the Life.
And he walked away grieving because following Jesus would cost him the security he treasured.
Let that settle.
He did not walk away because Jesus had nothing to offer.
He walked away because he could not bear to surrender what he already possessed.
And before we judge him too quickly, perhaps we should ask ourselves a question.
What is the one thing Jesus could ask you to surrender that would make you hesitate?
Your reputation?
Your secret relationship?
Your bitterness?
Your financial security?
Your need to be admired?
The version of yourself you have spent years trying to convince everyone is real?
Sometimes the hardest thing to lay at the feet of Jesus is not something obviously sinful.
Sometimes it is something good that has become more important to us than God Himself.
Jesus then told His disciples how difficult it was for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven.
They were astonished.
In their world, prosperity could easily be mistaken for evidence of divine favor.
If someone wealthy, disciplined, and outwardly righteous struggled to enter the kingdom, who could possibly be saved?
Jesus answered with words that still rescue desperate sinners today.
“With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible.” — Matthew 19:26 (KJV)
There it is.
The Gospel beginning to break through the illusion of human achievement.
Salvation is not a trophy awarded to people who have successfully impressed God.
It is the work of a gracious God who accomplishes what sinners cannot accomplish for themselves.
And then Peter spoke.
“Behold, we have forsaken all, and followed thee; what shall we have therefore?” (Matthew 19:27, KJV)
Peter had a legitimate question.
The disciples really had left things behind to follow Jesus. Their sacrifices mattered. Jesus did not dismiss them or pretend their obedience was meaningless.
He assured them that their faithfulness would not be forgotten and spoke of the future restoration and eternal life (Matthew 19:28–29).
But immediately afterward came the warning.
“Many that are first shall be last; and the last shall be first.”
Why?
Because even genuine sacrifice can become infected with comparison.
Even sincere obedience can slowly become a demand for recognition.
Even people who have followed Jesus for years can begin measuring their worth by how much more they have done than someone else.
And Jesus was about to tell a story that would expose that dangerous attitude.
A landowner went out early in the morning to hire workers for his vineyard.
He agreed to pay the first group a denarius for the day.
Later, he hired more workers.
Then more.
And more.
Finally, around the eleventh hour, near the end of the working day, he found others still standing idle.
He asked why they had been there all day.
They answered that nobody had hired them.
So he sent them into his vineyard too.
Imagine those final workers.
They had spent the day waiting.
Watching other men get chosen.
Watching opportunities disappear.
Perhaps wondering whether they would return home with enough money to feed their families.
They were not necessarily lazy. The story gives their explanation plainly: nobody had hired them.
And then, when the day was nearly over, someone finally called them.
Someone gave them a place.
Someone offered them work when the opportunity seemed almost gone.
Evening came.
The landowner instructed his steward to pay the workers, beginning with those who had arrived last.
And something extraordinary happened.
The men who worked only about one hour received a full denarius.
The same amount promised to those who had labored all day.
Imagine the shock.
Imagine the relief.
Imagine a worker who expected almost nothing suddenly holding enough wages for a full day.
But then the first workers stepped forward.
They had endured the heat.
They had carried the heavier burden.
They had been there from the beginning.
Surely they would receive more.
But they also received a denarius.
Exactly what they had agreed upon.
And they began to complain.
“These last have wrought but one hour, and thou hast made them equal unto us, which have borne the burden and heat of the day.” (Matthew 20:12, KJV)
Notice the words.
“Thou hast made them equal unto us.”
That was the wound.
Not that the landowner had failed to keep his promise.
He had kept it.
Not that the first workers had been cheated.
They had received the agreed wage.
Their anger rose because someone they considered less deserving had received the same generosity.
And now the story becomes painfully personal.
Because many of us can celebrate God's grace…
until that grace is extended to someone we believe deserves less than we do.
We love forgiveness when it covers our failures.
But when it reaches the person who wounded us, something inside us resists.
We rejoice when God restores our reputation.
But when He restores someone whose past is more scandalous than ours, we become suspicious.
We say that salvation is by grace.
Yet sometimes we behave as though grace should come with a ranking system.
The landowner answered one of the complaining workers:
“Friend, I do thee no wrong: didst not thou agree with me for a penny?” (Matthew 20:13, KJV)
The word “penny” in the King James Version refers here to a Roman denarius, not a modern penny.
Then came the piercing question.
“Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with mine own? Is thine eye evil, because I am good?” (Matthew 20:15, KJV)
That last question deserves more than a passing glance.
In the Greek text, the expression includes:

ὁ ὀφθαλμός σου πονηρός ἐστιν
ho ophthalmos sou ponēros estin
Literally, the question speaks of one's eye being evil.
But within the biblical world, an “evil eye” could describe an attitude of envy, resentment, or stinginess.
The meaning is not that the worker had a physically diseased eye.
Jesus was exposing the way envy can distort a person's vision.
The worker looked at another man's blessing and saw an injustice, even though he himself had received exactly what was promised.
The problem was not the landowner's goodness.
The problem was the worker's inability to rejoice in it.
And perhaps that is why this parable still hurts.
Because sometimes we are not angry that God has been unfaithful to us.
We are angry that He has been generous to somebody else.
Somebody who started later.
Somebody who made worse decisions.
Somebody who seems to have escaped consequences we had to endure.
Somebody who came to Christ after years of rebellion while we have been trying to obey Him for decades.
And hidden beneath our disappointment is a question we are almost afraid to admit.
Lord, why should they receive what I have spent my whole life working toward?
But Jesus never taught that eternal life could be purchased with enough years of religious service.
The Greek word translated “grace” in passages such as Ephesians 2:8 is χάρις (charis), expressing grace or favor.
Paul wrote:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV)
A gift.
Not a paycheck.
Not a spiritual promotion.
Not a certificate declaring that we outperformed other sinners.
A gift.
And that changes everything.
The thief on the cross did not have decades to serve in ministry.
He could not travel the world preaching.
He could not spend years making restitution.
He could not build a church or develop an impressive religious reputation.
He was dying.
His opportunities were disappearing with every breath.
And yet, beside him hung the Savior of the world.
The thief acknowledged his guilt, recognized Jesus' innocence, and pleaded:
“Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.” (Luke 23:42, KJV)
Jesus answered:
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” (Luke 23:43, KJV)
Think about that.
A condemned man.
A ruined reputation.
A life reaching its final moments.
And mercy met him there.
Not because his crimes were insignificant.
Not because repentance made the consequences of his past unreal.
Not because good works were unnecessary for those who still had a lifetime to live.
But because the crucified Christ had the authority to save a repentant sinner who could bring Him nothing except faith and a desperate plea for mercy.
This is not permission to postpone repentance.
Nobody is promised a final opportunity like that thief received.
It is proof that no sinner should assume the mercy of Jesus is too small to reach them.
And this is where the phrase “the last shall be first” becomes both a warning and a breathtaking invitation.
In Matthew 20:16, the Greek reads:
Οὕτως ἔσονται οἱ ἔσχατοι πρῶτοι καὶ οἱ πρῶτοι ἔσχατοι.
Houtōs esontai hoi eschatoi prōtoi kai hoi prōtoi eschatoi.
“So the last shall be first, and the first last.”
The word ἔσχατοι (eschatoi) means “last,” while πρῶτοι (prōtoi) means “first.”
Jesus deliberately reverses the order people expect.
But we must understand what He is saying in context.
He is not teaching that every person who becomes a Christian late in life automatically receives a greater reward than every lifelong believer.
He is not saying that diligence is worthless, that faithfulness does not matter, or that God ignores the sacrifices of His people.
Elsewhere, Scripture clearly teaches that God sees faithful service and will judge justly (1 Corinthians 3:8; Hebrews 6:10).
Nor is the parable a universal rule for how employers must calculate wages.
Its primary purpose is to reveal the surprising generosity of the kingdom of heaven and confront the pride that resents God's grace toward others.
The first workers were not wrong to work all day.
They were wrong to treat the landowner's generosity as an offense against themselves.
And that distinction matters.
Because the Gospel does not make obedience meaningless.
The Gospel changes why we obey.
We do not obey Jesus to purchase His love.
We obey because, through His grace, we have been brought into a relationship with Him.
We do not serve to prove that we deserve salvation.
We serve because the Savior who rescued us is worthy of our lives.
We do not give so that God will owe us a blessing.
We give because everything we possess ultimately belongs to Him.
And we do not measure our holiness by comparing ourselves with the people we believe are behind us.
We look to Christ.
The One who is holy.
The One who is righteous.
The One who is worthy.
And here is something even more astonishing.
The same Gospel of Matthew that records Jesus saying the first will be last also records Him explaining greatness in the kingdom.
“Whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant.” (Matthew 20:27, KJV)
Then He revealed the pattern behind that command.
“Even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.” (Matthew 20:28, KJV)
Do you see it?
Jesus did not merely teach His disciples to abandon the world's obsession with status.
He embodied the opposite way of life.
The rightful King came as a servant.
The sinless One washed the feet of sinners.
The Lord of glory endured humiliation.
The One worthy of every throne carried a cross.
The One who deserved worship was mocked by those He came to save.
Philippians 2:6–8 describes Christ's willing humility, culminating in obedience unto death, even death on a cross.
And then Philippians 2:9 declares that God highly exalted Him.
Jesus' humiliation was not the defeat of His mission.
It was central to the mission He came to fulfill.
His sacrifice was not merely an inspiring example of humility.
It was the saving work through which sinners can be reconciled to God.
He gave His life as a ransom.
He bore our sins.
He rose again.
And through repentance and faith in Him, guilty people can receive forgiveness and new life.
That is why the kingdom of God cannot be understood through the ordinary human obsession with being first.
At the center of our faith stands a crucified and risen Savior.
Not a self-promoting celebrity.
Not a religious performer demanding applause.
Not a king who preserved His comfort while others suffered.
Jesus Christ.
The Servant-King.
And perhaps the deepest question is no longer, Why did Jesus say the first will be last?
Perhaps the question is:
Have I been following the Jesus who carried the cross, or have I been using His name to build a throne for myself?
That question reaches the preacher.
It reaches the worship leader.
It reaches the generous donor.
It reaches the church volunteer.
It reaches the Christian who has attended services for forty years.
And it reaches the person who has only recently begun praying again after a long season of running from God.
Because pride does not always announce itself loudly.
Sometimes it wears the clothing of faithfulness.
Sometimes it sounds like, “After everything I've done for this church, why wasn't I recognized?”
Sometimes it whispers, “I've lived better than that person. Why does God seem to be blessing them?”
Sometimes it appears when someone with a shameful past begins growing in Christ and we quietly hope they never become more spiritually fruitful than we are.
And sometimes pride hides inside our suffering.
We begin believing that because we have endured more than others, we are entitled to a greater portion of God's affection.
But the cross will not allow us to turn grace into a competition.
There is no sinner so respectable that he no longer needs mercy.
And there is no repentant sinner so disgraced that the blood of Jesus is insufficient to cleanse him.
Consider the apostle Paul.
Before his conversion, he persecuted the church.
He was not merely indifferent to Christianity.
He actively opposed the followers of Jesus.
Yet the risen Christ confronted him, and his life was transformed.
Later, Paul wrote:
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.” (1 Timothy 1:15, KJV)
And in the next verse, Paul explained that he had received mercy so that Christ might display His longsuffering as an example to future believers.
Paul did not erase the truth about his past.
He did not celebrate his former violence.
He did not pretend that grace made sin harmless.
He understood that mercy had reached someone who could never have earned it.
And that mercy transformed the direction of his life.
From persecutor to preacher.
From enemy of the church to servant of Christ.
From a man convinced of his own righteousness to a man who boasted in the grace of God.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by removing the need for repentance, accountability, or transformation.
But by redeeming people who turn to Him and giving them a future their past could never produce.
And perhaps that is why this message feels so personal.
Because somewhere in the world tonight, a father is sitting alone, wondering whether the damage he caused his family can ever be repaired.
A mother is silently crying because she believes she has failed her children.
A young man is struggling with a secret sin he has promised to abandon a hundred times.
A woman is returning to church after years of feeling too ashamed to walk through the doors.
An exhausted believer is wondering whether decades of unnoticed faithfulness have meant anything.
And someone who once loved Jesus deeply is staring at a Bible that has remained unopened for months.
To the person who feels spiritually last, hear this carefully.
Being far behind other people does not place you beyond the reach of Christ.
But you must not mistake His mercy for permission to remain in rebellion.
Jesus does not call us to admire grace from a distance.
He calls us to repent, believe, and follow Him.
He does not simply offer a better public image.
He gives new life.
And if you are the person who has been serving faithfully for years, hear this too.
Jesus has not forgotten your labor.
Your obedience is not meaningless.
Your sacrifices are not invisible.
The Bible says:
“For God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love, which ye have shewed toward his name…” (Hebrews 6:10, KJV)
That promise matters.
Especially when nobody thanks you.
Especially when your service happens behind closed doors.
Especially when the people you helped never acknowledge what it cost you.
But do not let your faithful service become a prison of resentment.
You can work in the vineyard all day and still lose the joy of being there if you spend your evening counting everyone else's wages.
What a heartbreaking possibility.
To spend years serving a generous Master…
and become angry because He is generous.
To be surrounded by mercy…
and become bitter because mercy reaches someone else.
To know the language of grace…
and secretly wish grace had stricter limits for other people.
Maybe that is the warning Jesus wants us to hear.
Not that God despises the first workers.
Not that He prefers laziness over diligence.
But that the people who have received His kindness must never begin imagining themselves the owners of it.
Grace belongs to God.
And His goodness is not diminished when He shares it with someone else.
If He restores a broken marriage, rejoice.
If He saves a former addict, rejoice.
If He forgives a repentant person with a terrible past, rejoice.
If He brings someone back after years of wandering, rejoice.
If He raises up a faithful servant nobody ever noticed, rejoice.
And if someone you once considered spiritually behind you begins growing in wisdom, humility, and love…
rejoice.
Because the kingdom of God is not a race to prove who deserves Jesus most.
It is a kingdom of people who would be lost without Him.
There is also another danger here.
Some people hear about the eleventh-hour workers and conclude that they can delay surrendering their lives to Christ.
They imagine they can spend their youth pursuing whatever they want, ignore the voice of God for decades, and turn to Jesus when they are old.
But the parable never promises that everyone will live to see the eleventh hour.
The workers who came late did not know when the landowner would call them.
And you do not know how many days remain in your life.
Scripture says:
“Behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation.” (2 Corinthians 6:2, KJV)
Not when the addiction becomes easier to surrender.
Not when the relationship becomes less complicated.
Not when your finances finally stabilize.
Not when you have finished enjoying the sins you already know are destroying you.
Now.
Because the grace of Jesus is too precious to treat as an emergency plan for a future we have not been promised.
And yet, if you are reading these words after years of spiritual failure, do not allow regret to convince you that repentance is pointless.
Come to Christ.
Confess the truth.
Stop defending what He is calling you to surrender.
Ask Him for mercy.
Trust in His death and resurrection.
And begin walking in the newness of life that He gives.
You may have wasted years.
You may have damaged relationships.
You may still need to face consequences, seek forgiveness, make restitution where appropriate, and rebuild trust patiently.
Grace does not erase those responsibilities.
But your past does not have to remain the master of your future.
Jesus Christ is a greater Savior than your sin is a master.
And when He changes a life, the story is not merely that someone became more religious.
The story is that someone who was spiritually dead has been made alive through Him.
Someone who was lost has been found.
Someone who had been hiding in shame has stepped into the light.
Someone who once ran from God has begun walking with Him.
And the glory belongs to Jesus.
Not to the person's willpower.
Not to the ministry that first reached them.
Not to the religious leader who guided them.
To Jesus.
Always Jesus.
This is why the mission of sharing the Gospel matters so much.
There are people on your Facebook friends list who may never enter a church this Sunday.
People who smile in their profile pictures while privately battling despair.
People who have quietly concluded that God wants nothing to do with them.
People who have confused the failures of Christians with the character of Christ.
And people who are so comfortable with outward religion that they have never truly confronted their need for repentance.
A single article cannot save anyone.
Only Jesus saves.
But the truth of His Word can be carried through ordinary conversations, shared messages, and the testimony of believers who refuse to keep His goodness to themselves.
So if this message has exposed something in your heart, don't let it become another article you read, agree with, and forget.
Take a moment to respond honestly.
You do not have to reveal private details to strangers to prove that your repentance is sincere. God sees what is happening in your heart.
But sometimes a humble confession becomes the beginning of an encouraging conversation, a prayer, or a testimony that reminds another person they are not alone.
And consider tagging a friend or family member who would be encouraged by the reminder that God's mercy is not exhausted and that faithful service is never forgotten.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to expose their struggles.
But to invite them toward the hope found in Jesus Christ.
That is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a personality around a ministry.
Not to sell access to the grace that Jesus freely gives.
But to keep placing Scripture-centered encouragement, biblical teaching, and discipleship resources in front of people who are hungry for truth.

If you have never explored these resources, we warmly invite you to become part of a community that values biblical nourishment, spiritual maturity, repentance, healing, accountability, and the transforming power of the Gospel.
Not because following a page makes anyone a disciple.
But because repeated encounters with Scripture can encourage us to open our Bibles, examine our hearts, and keep looking to Christ.
And for those who want to help sustain and expand this work, there is another meaningful way to participate.
It is a voluntary expression of generosity toward a ministry you believe is serving others.
God's grace cannot be purchased.
And nobody should ever feel that they must pay money to prove their love for Jesus.
Not every believer can contribute financially, and that does not make their faith or love any less valuable.
A sincere prayer matters.
A thoughtful comment matters.
A message shared with someone who needs encouragement matters.
Stay.
Read.
Pray.
Grow.
Share what is true.
Keep opening your Bible.
Keep following Jesus.
It is to see people grow in the knowledge of Jesus Christ, stand firmly upon His Word, and live lives transformed by His grace.
One day, the applause of this world will fall silent.
The follower counts will mean nothing.
The titles will lose their power.
The recognition people spent their lives chasing will no longer define them.
And everything hidden behind our carefully maintained appearances will be exposed before the God who sees the heart.
On that day, our confidence must not rest in how important we became, how much attention we attracted, or how many people considered us successful.
Our hope must rest in Jesus Christ.
The Savior who died for sinners.
The Lord who rose from the grave.
The King who will judge with perfect righteousness.
The One whose mercy no human being can earn and whose holiness no human being can manipulate.
So stop asking whether you are ahead of everyone else.
Ask whether you are following Jesus.
Stop measuring your faithfulness by another person's failures.
Ask whether your own heart is becoming more like Christ.
Stop resenting the mercy that reaches people you once looked down upon.
Remember how desperately you needed that same mercy.
And when someone who has been wandering finally comes home to the Father, do not stand outside counting how many years you have been faithful.
Rejoice that the lost has been found.
Because the greatest miracle in the vineyard is not that the last workers received more than they expected.
It is that the Master was generous enough to call them at all.
And the greatest wonder of your salvation is not that you became better than somebody else.
It is that Jesus loved you while you were still a sinner and gave Himself to redeem you.
If this message has reached a place in your heart that you have kept hidden for years, take it to God in prayer.

“Lord Jesus, forgive me for the times I have compared myself with others. Forgive me for the pride I have disguised as faithfulness and the resentment I have allowed to grow when You showed mercy to someone else. Thank You for Your sacrifice on the cross and Your victory over death. Teach me to trust Your grace, repent sincerely, obey Your Word, and rejoice when others experience Your goodness. Give me a servant's heart. Let my life point people toward You rather than toward myself. And when I am tempted to seek the first place, remind me that following You is worth more than all the applause this world could offer. Amen.”
And remember this when you close the article:
You may have spent your whole life trying to be first, only to discover that the greatest place you could ever occupy was at the feet of Jesus.
